extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, scientists, and educated general readers interested in natural history and evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and difficulties that a theory of descent with modification must address (e.g., absence of transitional forms, origins of complex organs and instincts, hybrid sterility, causes of variation). Useful for evaluating the explanatory adequacy of evolutionary hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion and intermediate forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts or organs of an important and uniform nature occasionally varying so as to acquire, in some degree, the character of the same part or organ in an allied species; cases of forms intermediate between two other forms which themselves are doubtfully ranked as either varieties or species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives many instances (horses, asses, zebras, pigeons, hybrids) showing stripes and other markings reappearing by simple variation or in hybrids; he regards such occurrences as strong evidence that related species can re-express ancient characters (reversion/atavism). He notes a large collected list but cannot reproduce all cases in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same laws of variation for varieties and species
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever we have the means of instituting a comparison, the same laws appear to have acted in producing the lesser differences between varieties of the same species, and the greater differences between species of the same genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats similarity of the processes that produce varieties and species as a key expectation of descent-with-modification; any theory should account for this continuity of variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of external conditions (climate and food)
rubrics_metrics.description: The external conditions of life, as climate and food, etc., seem to have induced some slight modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External environment is credited with inducing minor changes; a satisfactory theory must allow for such influences while recognizing their limited explanatory reach for large modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of habit, use, and disuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Habit in producing constitutional differences, and use in strengthening, and disuse in weakening and diminishing organs, seem to have been more potent in their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites habit and the effects of use/disuse as important mechanisms that interact with variation and selection; a theory should integrate these effects when explaining modifications of structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homologous parts vary similarly and cohere
rubrics_metrics.description: Homologous parts tend to vary in the same way, and homologous parts tend to cohere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recurring parallel variation of homologous structures among related species is presented as evidence of common descent and must be explained by any account of morphological change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of growth (changes in one part affect others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications in hard parts and in external parts sometimes affect softer and internal parts. When one part is largely developed, perhaps it tends to draw nourishment from the adjoining parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasizes correlated changes in development as a constraint and driver of morphological change; theories should address covariation and developmental correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability of multiple (repeated) parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple parts are variable in number and in structure, perhaps arising from such parts not having been closely specialised to any particular function, so that their modifications have not been closely checked by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less-specialised, repeated structures are more labile; an account of variation should predict where variability is concentrated in the organism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater variability in less-specialized (lower) organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: It is probably from this same cause that organic beings low in the scale of nature are more variable than those which have their whole organisation more specialised, and are higher in the scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect greater phenotypic variability among organisms with less specialised organisation; this pattern is a testable implication of Darwin's view of variation and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary organs tend to be variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudimentary organs, from being useless, will be disregarded by natural selection, and hence probably are variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence and variability of rudimentary organs are seen as predictable under a theory of descent and selection, since selection does not constrain them strongly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific characters more variable than generic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific characters—that is, the characters which have come to differ since the several species of the same genus branched off from a common parent—are more variable than generic characters, or those which have long been inherited, and have not differed within this same period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction between recently acquired (specific) and long-inherited (generic) characters yields expectations about which traits remain labile versus fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Why, if species have descended from other species by insensibly fine gradations, do we not everywhere see innumerable transitional forms? Why is not all nature in confusion instead of the species being, as we see them, well defined?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin answers with multiple factors: extinction by competitive replacement, the extreme imperfection and intermittence of the geological record, former geographic fragmentation, narrow neutral zones between species where intermediates would be rare, smaller population sizes of intermediates leading to greater chance of extermination, and the tendency of common forms to present more favourable variations and supplant intermediates. Any evaluation must consider these processes when judging the expected visibility of transitional forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions in habits of life (origin of novel habits)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the origin and transitions of organic beings with peculiar habits and structure: e.g., how could a land carnivorous animal be converted into one with aquatic habits, or an insectivorous quadruped into a flying bat?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues by analogy and examples (Mustela vison, gradations among squirrels to flying squirrels, Galeopithecus, various bird wing-forms) that intermediate grades of habit and structure exist or have existed and that gradual accumulation of useful modifications can produce large shifts in habit. A theory must show plausible intermediate functional stages and their selective advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organs of extreme perfection and means of transition
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it possible that natural selection could produce... organs of such wonderful structure, as the eye, of which we hardly as yet fully understand the inimitable perfection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin contends transitional grades for highly perfected organs will seldom survive to the present and will be rare in the fossil record, but he presents diverse functional intermediates in wings (flappers, fins, sails, functionless vestiges) as evidence that multiple routes of gradual improvement are possible; thus explanations must supply plausible adaptive series of intermediate forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instincts: acquisition and modification by natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Can instincts be acquired and modified through natural selection? Example posed: the marvellous instinct which leads the bee to make cells, which have practically anticipated the discoveries of profound mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin raises this as a major difficulty (treated in a separate chapter) and implies that a satisfactory theory must account for complex, apparently 'designed' instincts by cumulative selection acting on slight hereditary modifications in behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterility of hybrids between species vs fertility of varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: How can we account for species, when crossed, being sterile and producing sterile offspring, whereas, when varieties are crossed, their fertility is unimpaired?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raised as a distinct difficulty (to be discussed separately); a plausible theory must explain differential hybrid fertility as a consequence of divergence and reproductive isolation processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharp species boundaries shaped by biotic interactions and range dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Although climate and height or depth graduate away insensibly, the range of any one species... will tend to be sharply defined (because of presence of other species, competition, predation, prey relationships), and intermediate varieties will often inhabit narrow neutral territories and be numerically rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses geographic distribution patterns and biotic competition to explain why species remain well-defined rather than forming continuous blends; evaluations should weigh ecological interactions and demographic effects when assessing the plausibility of continuous vs discrete taxonomic patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population size and area influence likelihood of further modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms existing in larger numbers will always have a better chance, within any given period, of presenting further favourable variations for natural selection to seize on, than will the rarer forms which exist in lesser numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin points out that common, widespread forms are more likely sources of further adaptive variation and hence will tend to outcompete and supplant rarer intermediate forms; theories should incorporate stochastic and sampling effects of population size.
